title: Social media habits
paragraphs: A recent survey of 500 students at five Kazakhstani universities — including WKU — found that the average student spends four hours and twenty minutes per day on social media platforms. That is more than thirty hours per week, or roughly sixty full days per year. When these statistics were shared with the students themselves, the most common reaction was a mixture of shock, recognition, and laughter. "I knew it was a lot," said one third-year student, "but not that much."

Instagram is the most popular platform among WKU students, used by 87% of respondents. Students use it primarily for entertainment — following accounts related to fashion, fitness, food, travel, and humour. However, a growing number also use Instagram for professional purposes: building a personal brand, showcasing their artwork or photography, and following industry leaders in their chosen career fields. "My Instagram is half dance videos and half computer science news," says Amir, smiling. "I am still figuring out my brand."

YouTube comes in a close second, used by 82% of students. Its role in student life is different from Instagram — students rely on YouTube heavily for educational content. Programming tutorials, maths explanations, language learning channels, and university lecture recordings all form part of the modern student's study toolkit. Many students say they prefer watching a fifteen-minute YouTube explanation to re-reading three pages of a textbook. "If my textbook had a 'skip to 2x speed' button, I'd be very happy," joked one student.

Telegram is essential for day-to-day university life. Every student group has its own Telegram channel or group chat where important announcements, lecture notes, homework deadlines, and last-minute schedule changes are shared instantly. Some professors communicate exclusively through Telegram. "If you are not on Telegram, you might as well not be in university," says Kamila, only half-joking. Unlike Instagram, which students use by choice, Telegram is practically a compulsory tool for academic survival.

TikTok is the platform that generates the most debate. Its short video format — usually between fifteen seconds and three minutes — is perfectly designed to capture and hold attention. Many students say they "accidentally" spend one to two hours on TikTok because the algorithm is so good at showing them content they enjoy. The platform's impact on concentration is controversial: some researchers say it shortens attention spans and makes focused studying harder. Others point out that TikTok has a surprisingly active educational community — some of the most popular creators explain complex science, history, and language topics in under sixty seconds.

Twitter (now rebranded as X) and Facebook are rarely used by students under the age of twenty-five. "Facebook is for my parents and TikTok is for my younger siblings," says Rustam with a grin. LinkedIn is gaining popularity among students in their third and fourth years as they begin thinking about careers and internships. Students who use LinkedIn regularly say it has helped them discover job opportunities and connect with professionals in their field.

The survey also asked about negative effects. The top three problems reported were: difficulty concentrating during study sessions (64%), disrupted sleep due to late-night phone use (58%), and feelings of anxiety or inadequacy caused by comparing themselves to others on social media (47%). Perhaps the most telling finding was this: 71% of students said they wanted to use social media less, but only 23% had actually tried to limit their usage in the past month.

What does this tell us? Social media is not going away — and frankly, for a university student in 2026, trying to live entirely without it would be both impractical and isolating. The real challenge is to develop what researchers call "digital literacy": the skill of using technology critically, purposefully, and in a way that serves your goals rather than distract from them. As Kamila puts it: "I want social media to be my tool, not my master."

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: Kamila, be honest — how much time do you spend on Instagram every day?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: I checked my screen time last week... it was two and a half hours a day. I was horrified!

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: Mine was three hours! Mostly TikTok. The algorithm just knows exactly what I want to watch.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: That's the problem — it's designed to keep you scrolling. Do you ever feel worse after using it?

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: Sometimes, yeah. I see other footballers who are much more talented and I think... why bother?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: That's the comparison trap. I do the same thing with language learners — they all seem so fluent!

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: So what do you do about it? Have you tried a digital detox?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: I set app limits on my phone — Instagram is blocked after 30 minutes. It sends me a warning.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Mostly yes! Except I sometimes just... override the limit. But it makes me aware of the time.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: I need to do that. The worst is using TikTok in bed — I never fall asleep before 1 am.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Same problem as Amir! Honestly, the whole generation has the same bad habits.

grammarNote:
Present Simple + выражения частотности — мощная комбинация для описания регулярных действий. Ты уже знаешь наречия (always, usually...). Теперь добавляем ВЫРАЖЕНИЯ частотности.

📌 ДВА ТИПА выражений частотности:

① НАРЕЧИЯ (перед основным глаголом, после "be"):
always · usually · often · sometimes · rarely · never
"I always check my phone." · "She is never late."

② ВЫРАЖЕНИЯ ЧАСТОТНОСТИ (обычно в конце предложения):
every day / every morning / every week / every month / every year
once a week / twice a month / three times a year
on Mondays / at weekends / in the evenings
"I exercise three times a week."
"She checks her email twice a day."
"We have English on Mondays and Wednesdays."

📍 ПОЗИЦИЯ в предложении:
① Наречия — ПЕРЕД глаголом: "I often visit her."
② Выражения — ПОСЛЕ глагола/дополнения: "I visit her twice a month."

🔢 КАК СТРОИТЬ выражения частотности:
once = один раз → once a week, once a month
twice = два раза → twice a week, twice a day
three times, four times... → three times a year
every + период → every day, every Monday, every summer

💡 Сравни: наречие vs выражение:
"I usually go to the gym." (наречие — насколько регулярно)
"I go to the gym three times a week." (выражение — конкретная частота)

⚠️ Ошибки:
❌ "I go every days." → ✅ "I go every day." (без -s после every!)
❌ "twice times a week" → ✅ "twice a week" (без "times" с once/twice!)
❌ "I three times go." → ✅ "I go three times a week." (выражение в конце!)
